original_question: Let A \subset \mathbb{R}^d be a compact totally disconnected set for which there exist at least two different Steiner trees connecting A (call them S and T). A maximal distance minimizer (also called an r-minimizer) for a compact set M \subset \mathbb{R}^d is a connected compact set \Sigma of minimal length (one-dimensional Hausdorff measure H^1(\Sigma)) among connected compact sets satisfying M \subset B_r(\Sigma), where B_r(\Sigma) is the closed r-neighborhood of \Sigma. Can one of the Steiner trees (for example S) also arise as a solution to a maximal distance minimization problem (for some choice of r > 0 and some compact target set M)?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.1 in the introduction: the finite-point inverse-minimizer conjecture characterizing exactly which Steiner trees can occur as maximal distance minimizers for n-point targets, framed against Proposition 1.2 and Theorem 1.3.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper’s inverse-maximal-distance-minimizer theme, uses the right notion of an r-minimizer, and focuses on the key obstruction suggested by the paper: nonuniqueness of the Steiner tree. It also correctly asks whether a Steiner tree can arise as a maximal distance minimizer for some choice of target set and radius.
missing_details: The paper’s target is not an arbitrary compact totally disconnected terminal set A, but a finite labeled terminal n-tuple A=(A_1,...,A_n). This finite-point restriction is essential in the relevant discussion in Section 3.1.
The target set M in the relevant inverse problem is likewise an n-tuple of points, not an arbitrary compact set. Your draft broadens M beyond the paper’s setup.
The paper’s nearest official formulation is an if-and-only-if characterization, not just the one-direction question 'can a nonunique Steiner tree occur?'.
The paper explicitly includes the quantifier 'for some small enough positive r'; this small-r regime is part of the intended formulation.

The nearby results distinguish a proved positive direction under a topological-stability hypothesis (Theorem 1.3 / Section 3.1 Theorem 3.3) from a proved negative direction in the planar full-tree nonunique case (Proposition 1.2 / Section 3.1 Proposition 3.4). Your draft does not record either restriction.
The planar negative result requires the tree to be full and nonunique, and the ambient dimension to be 2. Those are paper-critical restrictions for the necessity result.

Theorem 1.3 is stated for labeled topology: every Steiner tree for an n-tuple in the closed 2r-neighborhood of A must have the same topology as St. This is the precise sufficient condition used nearby.

The paper’s motivating formulation is about Steiner trees for finitely many terminals, not Steiner trees for general compact totally disconnected sets with possibly infinitely many branching phenomena.
No algebraic ambient field, homogeneity, degree, or nilpotency data are relevant here; the missing details are geometric/variational quantifiers and finite-vs-compact scope restrictions instead.
refined_question: Let A=(A_1,...,A_n) be a finite labeled set of points in R^d, and let St be a Steiner tree for A, i.e. a connected compact set of minimal H^1-length among connected compact sets containing A. For r>0 and compact M subset R^d, call Sigma an r-minimizer for M if Sigma is connected and compact, M is contained in the closed r-neighborhood of Sigma, and H^1(Sigma) is minimal among all such connected compact competitors. Is it true that St is an r-minimizer for some n-tuple M=(M_1,...,M_n) of points and some sufficiently small r>0 if and only if St is the unique Steiner tree for its terminal set A?
justification: The draft is trying to capture the paper’s inverse-minimizer question for Steiner trees, but it broadens both the terminal set A and the target set M beyond the paper’s actual scope. In the paper, this issue is formulated in the finite-point setting: Section 3.1 explains the inverse problem for finite M, states the positive sufficient criterion (Theorem 3.3) and the planar negative result for nonunique full trees (Proposition 3.4), while the introduction packages the intended open problem as Conjecture 1.1, with Proposition 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 as the immediately adjacent partial results. So the sharp, paper-faithful question is the finite n-point iff characterization, not the broader compact totally disconnected variant.
